subtopic: INFLATION-COST OF LIVING INCREASE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
INFLATION-COST OF LIVING INCREASE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion under Standing Order 43 to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely, the accelerated rate of increase of the consumer price index-the cost of living-during February, which raised the general level of prices in Canada 5 per cent above the level of a year ago, and particularly, the refusal of the government to apply sanctions against those who raise prices by more than the government's guideline, thus enabling sellers to continue to raise prices by whatever amount they desire, and making impossible the control of inflation.
I therefore move the following motion under Standing Order 43:
That this House, comprising the elected representatives of all the people of Canada, consider and recommend a more effective method of controlling and keeping within reasonable bounds the accelerating increase in the cost of living.

The Canadian provisional offer of tariff preferences for imports of manufactured and semi-manufactured goods from developing countries, along with the offers of other prospective donors, is still being discussed internationally both in the OECD and the UNCTAD. subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on Thursday evening, and having spent some 25 minutes in comment upon his budget I find, on reviewing the remarks I made at that time, they were more accurate than I could have dreamed. I wish, first, to briefly recapitulate my remarks on the nature of the budget.
First of all, I think we will agree that the intensity of inflation today is due in large measure to the failure of the federal government and the provinces to settle priorities for the main government spending programs, particularly in the fields of health, education and social welfare. Second, we would agree that the government's monetary and fiscal measures have not had any noticeable effect on inflation up to the present time. This is evidenced by the present level of interest rates and continually rising prices. Today, we have a clear indication of a further rise in prices, and the monetary and fiscal measures which were supposed to be so effective have failed to make any impression whatsoever on what we consider to be the main yardstick of inflation.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I think it is also agreed that the monetary and fiscal measures of the government are causing an economic slowdown, and this is evidenced by rising unemployment. So, we have this strange paradox that we are in a highly inflationary period, with interest rates at an all time high, and we are building up more and more unemployment.
The third point I made was with respect to control of government expenditures. In his budget speech, and again on television, the minister laboured to emphasize that he and his colleagues have got their expenditure programs under control. Frankly, that is more apparent than real. After all, Mr. Speaker, the estimates for 1969-70 showed an increase
March 16. 1970

The Budget-Hon. M. Lambert in federal government expenditures of $1 billion-$1,000 million dollars-and the estimates tabled the other day for 1970-71, without taking into account any supplementary estimates which may be filed, already provide for a further increase of $900 million. If that is having our programs under control, then I wonder what it would be like if they were not under control? After all, the mammoth cut-backs announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last summer for certain departments, and particularly the personnel of those departments, are frankly non-existent. When you increase spending programs by $800 million or $900 million in your main estimates, with anywhere up to a quarter million dollars coming in on your supplementary estimates, then there is no question but that the government has not got the spending programs under control.
I wonder whether we will get further indications from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) or anybody else representing the government that certain open-ended programs such as medicare, post-secondary education, hospital insurance and the Canada Assistance Plan will be blamed. Those programs were blamed by the President of the Treasury Board the last time he made his confession that the government's figures were wildly in error.
The next item I referred to was the consumer credit controls which will have the most effect on the consumer durables, with the highest incidence in Ontario and Quebec. This is a strange method of fighting present day inflation, by reverting to the means used at the time of the Korean conflict in 1950-52 when inflation was of a different sort. We know that at that time there were too few goods and services chased by far too much money but today the dollars are not chasing too few goods because, in some lines, there are distressingly high inventories. I will admit there is a fair amount of money in certain sectors but in others, for instance in western agriculture and among the lower income groups there is not that much money. Yet what we are to be asked is to encourage more unemployment and have more economic slack because those results would flow from consumer credit controls.
Then, there is the failure to fight high unemployment in the textile industry by not implementing the recommendations of the Tariff Board which were in the minister's hands in ample time for decision and action in the budget.

The next item is the failure to provide relief against inflation for persons on low income and for old age pensioners by granting them an increment to the general income supplement. This, in itself, need not make such heavy inroads on the revenue of the government because some form of tax credit could be granted, as spoken of by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) for persons with low incomes, that is those with any other form of revenue than old age pension.
I did say that we agreed with the minister's proposal with regard to water and air pollution control but that is about the only part of the budget we approve.
On the basis of my remarks the other night, Mr. Speaker, I move:
That all the words after "House" be deleted and there be added the following:
Regrets that the budgetary proposals of the government fail to provide any tax relief for persons of low income, fail to recommend any increase in the guaranteed income supplement to the old age security pension, and those which impose consumer credit controls will not only fail to curb inflation but will contribute materially to increasing unemployment.

subsubtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to return to the question of consumer credit controls. The minister has indicated that he wishes to consult with credit granting institutions of one kind or another and then bring in his regulations in six or eight weeks. This is an odd way of doing this because, in the interval, there could be such a splurge of buying in certain lines that an artificial shortage could be created and you would have a continuing pressure on the commodities in question. In other lines, there could be an exhaustion of the demand for many months to come because of a tendency to buy ahead of time. Therefore, you would have a complete and utter slack in those particular industries or areas which provided services.
We do not know what kind of controls we are going to get and depending on the nature of these controls there may be all sorts of evasions. In the weekend press we read suggestions for getting around some types of consumer credit control. When we look at the auto industry, which is a basic industry, we know it certainly will be the bellwether as to the level of prosperity in the country. At the weekend the president of Ford of Canada indicated that sales across Canada were down
March 16, 1970	COMMONS
20 to 25 per cent as a whole for that company, and I am sure that they are in the same position as all the other motor companies. We have seen that motor car sales have varied from a decrease of 16 per cent to perhaps a bit more than 30 per cent since January 1. Why would the minister want to impose consumer credit controls on that industry which is already suffering a one-third decrease in volume. This is quite incomprehensible. It is also incomprehensible that the down payment should be limited to 20 per cent and that the maximum repayment period should be 30 months.
In this morning's Gazette there is an item cited by John Meyer, which shows that in the Montreal area the average down payment for automobiles is 25 per cent, which is more than will be required under the controls. It also states that the maximum average repayment period is 29 months. This is less than is proposed by the government but still there is inflation, there is no doubt about that. It is incomprehensible that in an industry which is already suffering from a decline in sales, the minister would introduce consumer credit controls in order to control inflation. His terms of repayment and the amount of the down payment are actually lower than those prevailing in the industry. Does he think that under his proposals there is going to be any greater control? Hardly. In arriving at these figures of 20 per cent down with a maximum of 30 months repayment period, I should like to know if the government has tested the situation in the Toronto-Hamilton area, for instance, or Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton, Vancouver or Halifax to see if these figures are not actually less than the conditions prevailing in the market. If so, the whole exercise would be completely an exercise in futility with no results whatsoever and this is what I wanted to know.

Another point with regard to consumer credit controls is this: they strike at purchasers from all income levels. The automobile dealer or furniture store dealer selling consumer wares will not ask the potential purchaser, "Are you earning $6,000 or $9,000 a year, or $15,000?" I suppose the requirement for a down payment would then depend on what the customer is earning. Yet is it not true that an across the board requirement for a 20 per cent or more than 20 per cent down payment will affect the man earning $6,000 a year far more than the man earning $15,000 or $20,000? Therefore, who is hit again by

There are two other points I should like to make. In the report, there is the same note of caution sounded. I refer now to the testimony introduced by the Governor of the Bank of Canada I refer hon. members to page 10 of the report. There is also a section on incomes, productivity and prices on the same page which I would commend to hon. members. This is part of a recommendation, and I shall quote from it very briefly.
We were particularly interested in the view that labour and management in certain key industries referred to by Galbraith as the "industrial heartland" agreed to wage settlements perhaps at times no greater than their own productivity increases but greater than the average productivity increase for the economy. Such a practice would have the effect of encouraging other less productive industries to follow the wage pattern of the pace-setting industries. When such wage settlements are accompanied by corresponding price increases there is an inflationary cost-push. We recommend that a study in depth be undertaken of the influence of wages and prices in key industries on the Canadian economy. Similarly, the importance of the service industries, employing about 50 per cent of the labour force, seems little understood as a factor in inflation. We think more research is needed.
In the light of this recommendation and many others along similar lines, I would have expected some indication from the government that it would direct the attention of the Economic Council to this question. How does one measure productivity in actual fact, particularly in the service industries? It is very simple to determine productivity levels in industries which produce goods, and to ascertain whether increased productivity is, or is not, the equivalent of wage increases. One can determine the effect of changes in levels of wages and productivity. We have had considerable experience in doing this. But with regard to the service industries we encounter obvious difficulties. For instance, my hon. friend from Calgary North might increase his fees as a lawyer, or my hon. friend from Orillia might increase his medical fees. But how can we tell whether there has been a corresponding increase in productivity? Of course, I am pulling the leg of my hon. friend from Calgary. But how can we tell whether an increase is justifiable?
For example, how can productivity in the field of education be measured? There have certainly been great increases in salaries in the educational field. Has there been a corresponding increase in productivity? It is an entirely unknown subject, but the impact of changes of this kind on the Canadian economy is immense. It is noteworthy that in the

The housing crisis in Canada is worsening year by year. Housing starts this year are way down. Some houses are just being completed, but the projection is that housing starts this year will be down compared with last year, and the inevitable result will be that rents will rise to even higher levels than they are at the present time. In face of this situation, the budget, in effect, tells the nation: "Don't worry about housing. The government will make a little money available in the public sector, but there is nothing or very little for housing in general in Canada".
We are living in an environment that is being polluted. People who are examining the problem are warning us that our society, our civilization, our very lives are in danger if we do not do something to stop pollution. Yet this budget continues to grant 50 per cent write-offs to industry, for anti-pollution devices, perpetuating the practice of the past. This has been found an inadequate measure because it does not really deal with the problem or with the urgency of the situation. There is so little in this budget that the government had to grasp at these meagre, minor items in order to show that some matters at least have been given thought. But thinking is not enough; we have to do something about our problems. This budget gives no indication of any conception of the task ahead of us.
Our urban municipalities are in desperate need. As far as they are concerned, the budget says, in effect: "Tough luck; the government has other priorities". There is no recognition in the budget of those problems that face urban society, a society in which the majority of the people in Canada live. Are we going to wait until our cities are destroyed before the government takes action? Can we not learn anything from looking at the situation of cities in North America, where some are already virtually destroyed and the cost of recovery is almost beyond comprehension? Although time is on our side in Canada, it will not continue to be with budgets of this kind.
While the government takes pride-or so it says-in increasing its expenditure on regional development, it cuts its own throat and sabotages its own efforts by maintaining a high level of unemployment, creating particu-

lar problems in disadvantaged regions of Canada. The government might just as well throw money down the drain. We do not begrudge the money spent on regional development; in fact, we think more should be spent. But the only way to make this expenditure effective is to have full employment. If you allow the economy to drag its feet at a time when you are pouring money into regional development, at best all you are doing is preventing the situation from getting worse. Certainly, you are not improving it.
How does one justify bringing in this kind of budget? I can say with a great deal of sadness that I never thought I would see a government in Canada bring in a budget proposal which, in the words of the budget, offered an invitation to union busting in Canada. Never before have I seen a budget that used such language, language which indicates that Canada is going to have labour strikes. It is as though the government wanted strikes to take place, as though the government is telling employers in this country to encourage strikes. This is something which is particularly incomprehensible. One of the members of the press gallery asked me why I was of this view. Now, Mr. Speaker, what should be done? What steps should the government take to deal with the deplorable economic and social situation in which we now live? Calling elections, replacing the federal government by a Progressive Conservative government, would make no difference. The Progressive Conservatives admit themselves that they have no solution. Before bringing my remarks to a close, Mr. Speaker, let me put forward Creditiste solutions. First of all, we suggest that the control and the issue of credit in Canada be removed from private banks which now have the power to finance the wealth of Canada, to create money and lend it to the government, instead of earning it.
First of all, the federal government should, through the Bank of Canada, control the money circulating in the country and do so by depriving the banks of a power which is not theirs but that of the people of Canada and of the government which is in turn responsible to the people.
We would like the Bank of Canada, a monetary body, to enable finance to reflect the Canadian reality and the Canadian wealth. The Bank of Canada ought to finance capital and public works at the administrative rate of J or J per cent.
The Bank of Canada should enable the provinces to finance bridges, highways, aqueducts, sidewalks, sewers, schools, gymnasiums, and so on. But no, our federal government is tied down to the task of serving the interests of big business thus compelling our public institutions, such as provincial governments, municipalities and schoolboards, to grovel before the big business tycoons and to pay interest rates up to 12, 14 and 15 per cent as such is now the case. Canadian citizens are now, by way of taxation, paying three times the price of every bridge, road, school, gymnasium, sidewalk, aqueduct, or sewer network which is built in the country.
It is high time, Mr. Speaker, to stop laughing at the Ralliement creditiste, for it is the only group in the House that has ever had the guts to put their fingers on the sore spot of finance. For instance, when private enterprise requires capital to expand and to increase production at a more reasonable cost, it has to borrow on the financial market. Why? Because the federal government does not authorize the public sector to put savings at the disposal of the private sector.
We know that some municipalities and school boards of the province of Quebec have now to borrow at a rate of 14 per cent. Provincial governments should unite and ask the federal government to change its financial system, because it no longer meets the provinces' needs. It is no longer in step with production which is not lacking for the time being.
In Canada, in 1969, production amounted to $79 billion, whereas an amount of $50 billion was paid out in wages and dividends of all kinds. How is it possible, with a purchasing power worth $50 billion, to use up production worth $79 billion? It is like trying to square the circle.
The Canadian people is left with the alternative of borrowing on their future, of mortgaging their future earnings and wages.
In 1960, our gross national product stood at $30 billion and in 1969 at $78 billion, which means that it has more than doubled during that period.
On the other hand, the national debt which amounted in 1960 to $20 billion increased at the end of 1969 to $39.9 billion. Production has doubled in 10 years, but so did the national debt.
The more the Canadians work, the more they develop the country and the more they go into debt. More and more, we are mortgaging our future, the future earnings, in order to live today, because according to the present system, the Canadian people are told: Buy today yesterday's production with tomorrow's money. Why? Because the purchasing power, the economic system, the financial power do not correspond to the production power. The Creditistes want to make the purchasing power equal to the production power.

In connection with this budget there are certain aspects upon which I should like to congratulate the government, and others upon which I will reserve judgment.
I should like to congratulate the government on the fact this is the first time in 13 years, I believe, when there have been no tax increases. I should also like to congratulate the government on the fact that this is the first time since 1956 that the government has balanced its budget and shown a surplus. This indicates good economic management. Third, I should like to congratulate the government on its attempt to hold the line in government spending and achieve greater efficiency in the public service.
The chief critic for the Conservative party declared that government spending was out of control. This is not the case. The figures show that expenditure which is purely under the control of the federal government increased by only 3.8 per cent last year, less than the total increase in the gross national product. It is true that the cost of programs which are shared with the provinces increased at a faster rate but, as we know, the federal government does not have full control over those programs. However, attempts are now being made to negotiate a system by which expenditures of this type can be better controlled.
I should further like to congratulate the government upon the priorities established in its spending programs. Looking at the estimates we can see the directions in which the government places its highest values. Provision is made for an increase of $52 million in the estimates of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion; there is an increase of $34 million in the sum available for programs for Indians and Eskimos; an increase of $21 million in the estimates for programs affecting manpower retraining; an increase of $12 million in provision for industrial incentives and development; the shift of $200 million into public housing, and an increase of $15 million in programs for external aid.
Examining these estimates we see that the emphasis has been placed on programs to relieve poverty both at home and abroad. Finally, I believe the government should be congratulated upon the initiative it took in producing incentives for the control of both water and air pollution. administration of unions and, third, measures to protect the unions themselves. I think all three areas are important if we are going to have a sound economy and a stable labour movement.
I should like to refer to some of the recommendations in that task force report because I thought it was an excellent report. To begin with, that report suggested that the Canadian Labour Relations Board be given greater discretion in determining the original bargaining unit, and changes in established bargaining units. It also suggested changes in union certification requirements and in successor rights provisions. If we had specific successor rights provisions in our law now, perhaps we would not be having some of the problems we do have in Montreal with the postal disputes. There, we have a classic case of problems which arise from succession rights of unions, where one bargaining unit is going to be replaced by five bargaining units, or five companies replacing one company.
Then, the task force had recommendations for the protection of the union members. It suggests union member protection from unreasonable initiation fees, dues and assessments; a "Bill of Rights" and independent judiciary for union members; regulation of conduct of ratification and strike votes; widened union accountability to employers, members and others, and regulation of union political expenditures.
Then there is a very good recommendation that there be a public interest disputes commission to assist in handling potential emergency disputes, and in particular to protect the interests of the public. Many people have felt that more should be done in this area. I do not know whether the public interest disputes commission would be the best way of protecting the public, but it is certain that in some labour disputes the public suffers more than either the employer or the employees and something should be done to protect them.
Another very good recommendation is that we have six months advance notice of industrial conversion causing permanent displacement. We have had several instances of that in Montreal. There was the Vickers case and there is a case now in Toronto-I forget the name of the company-where the workers in a tire factory are being laid off without sufficient notice.

We cannot always presume this action is based on labour greed or a quest for power by labour unions. We cannot make that presumption, as some people in this country have. When men resort to violence or illegal strikes, it is because in many cases they are afraid they are going to lose the jobs they have had for a long time or that they have a basic feeling of insecurity. They have seen other men who have worked for five, ten, 15 or 20 years on the job and then put out of work with hardly any notice and no compensation.
When men with families are faced with situations like these, they sometimes do not act as reasonable men. Sometimes they wildcat and sometimes cause violence. It is for this reason that in amending our labour legislation we have to try to put forward solutions which will not only deal with the symptoms but also with the causes. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as all hon. members know, in this budget debate we have freedom to cover the vast range of human concern with which a government of a vigorous nation must concern itself in a technological and complicated age. As always, we must recognize that within this House, as well as within our society generally, the old adage applies: A lot of today's frustration is caused by a surplus of simple answers coupled with a tremendous shortage of simple problems. Of this fact I am well aware.
There are no slick solutions to society's ills and no glib analysis within it. Those who assume that we can revert to a sort of primeval simplicity are still clinging to a rear-view mirror view of the world. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) has
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
DEBATES	March 16. 1970
pointed out in an excellent manner the basic concern that must face all hon. members who deal seriously with the budget issue; that is, if we want to spend more we have to tax more. We cannot simply demand more advantages from government without facing the situation of more taxation, or vice versa. I will not make any more reference to that aspect of the matter because it has already been dealt with by other hon. members. The hon. member seated directly in front of me did that capably earlier this afternoon.
It is inevitable in any society that the majority of the populace, if given a choice, will prefer to cling to that which is familiar, the familiar laws and traditions, even if they know them to be unjust, rather than risk the new because the new is always the unknown. Marshall McLuhan has reminded us that we are always one step behind in our view of the world because we are benumbed by any new technology.
Because of today's terrific speed-up of information, we have a chance to apprehend and to predict. Certainly the most exciting aspect of all is to influence the environmental forces controlling us and thus, in a certain sense, win back control of our own destinies. I should not use the term "win back" because I firmly believe if we look through the pages of human endeavour as far as history is concerned, we see that man has never controlled his own destiny: there have always been forces and factors beyond our control. But we do have technological levers and tools now at our disposal which give us a great potential to direct our own future.
I wish to spend some time referring to a few of the frustrations and issues which face a backbencher such as myself and perhaps also backbenchers on the other side of the House; indeed, some of them may apply to this country as a whole. First, I want to put on the record that in my opinion Members of Parliament from all parties work far harder, have more responsibilities and more opportunities for creative participation in policy than is generally believed, understood or known to the Canadian public. Second, there is in Canada a kind of a schizophrenic attitude toward elected members. On the one hand, the public seems to assume that Members of Parliament are a useless, self-seeking, lazy lot; on the other hand, we are confronted with the attitude of: Why don't you do more. Why don't you lobby, research and plan more? Why don't you participate more in the constituency, read more letters and represen-
March 16, 1970	COMMONS
tations, be better informed and prevent old errors from being perpetuated, stop favouritism, help us, defend motherhood and fight evil, etc.? All of these are important. I am sure all hon. members agree with this.
It is at this precise point that the stark irony comes into the situation. To pursue all of the opportunities and responsibilities that come to all members of this very distinguished chamber, we are granted the great machinery or equipment of one small cubbyhole for an office, a telephone and one secretary. We are then told by our constituents: Go to it fellows; you need to change the world.
In my own case I have upward of 60,000 constituents spread over more than 2,000 square miles. As hon. members know, there are approximately 17 major standing committees where, if time and research permitted, an hon. member could make a real and genuine contribution. To this we must add the numerous caucus study committees where a backbench Member of Parliament can have a real input in policy.
We are desperately limited in the information services that are available to communicate with our constituencies. It is difficult for a member to find time and indeed secretarial help to send sufficient information and to write an adequate number of letters to constituents. More limited still are the duplicating equipment facilities which must be used for providing information to constituents. We are not provided with proper equipment for this challenging and creative job. As far as communicating with the public is concerned, we are to all intents and purposes at the mercy of newspapers, in rural areas weeklies and in other areas dailies, and other media.
It is necessary for the newspapers to make a profit: they are running a business. These newspapers are governed by editors who are not even here. They are not elected and are therefore not responsible to the people in the same sense that we are. They cannot possibly adequately assess what is going on here unless we are to assume that remoteness from familiarity with the facts makes for objectivity. These are some of the frustrations I experience as a Member of Parliament.
Some hon. members know my professional background was as an agriculturist and, latterly, as a clergyman. The facilities in so far as equipment and space for secretarial staff that were available to me as a clergyman were far superior to those which are available to me as a Member of the House of Commons.

Yes. Mr. Speaker, it is impossible for me to understand how the myth has grown up that backbenchers have no opportunity to put forward their views. The sad truth, and I use that adjective purposely, is that these opportunities have become so numerous that the House and its committees are constantly subjected to views which demonstrate only one thing, namely, that most members have not had the time or the opportunity to place themselves in command of the relevant facts before offering their contributions to posterity via the Hansard record. Again, I do not hesitate to identify myself as one of the offenders here, because I hardly ever go to a committee meeting confident that I have done sufficient homework before I attend, or before I speak in the House. I suppose this occasion is no exception.
On December 15 of the present session- and here I turn to another subject-I was privileged to place a motion before this House for debate. The report of the debate appears at page 1981 and following pages of Hansard. The motion read as follows:
That in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to the advisability of including the counties of Renfrew and Lanark as a suitable and necessary extension of that portion of northeastern Ontario which is now a designated area under the provisions of the Regional Development Incentives Act.
As the House knows, last Wednesday this motion, together with other efforts put forth by my hon. friend from Renfrew North (Mr. Hopkins) and myself, bore fruit. Renfrew, Arnprior and Pembroke were declared special areas under the legislation establishing the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. For the purposes of this legislation, a special area is one in which special action is needed to promote economic expansion and social adjustment because employment opportunities are exceptionally inadequate either within the area itself or within the larger region of which the area forms a part.


Renfrew county is the largest county in Ontario. It has a significant potential in two directions especially-forest-based industries and tourism. It was primarily to enable the development of the forest-based industries that these locations were declared special areas. The benefits in growth and employment which will now accrue to the whole county will be limited only by the extent to which local, county and municipal representatives together with present and prospective industries take advantage of the opportunities which have now come to our region as a result of a lot of people working hard over a long period of time. To win half the case, or to get one pair of shoes only, is only half the battle and the needs of the child who remains shoeless must now receive all the more attention.
I turn now to another subject-Canada's participation in international population control programs. Most hon. members are aware, I suppose, that the Canadian Development Agency has begun talks with the International Planned Parenthood Federation, with officials of the United Nations organization which is concerned with control of population and with the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, as well as with the World Bank and other organizations which support programs of this type. Last evening it was my privilege to be in the town of Carleton Place to participate in a forum on some of the social needs of our nation. Those present saw a film that had

The Budget-Mr. McBride been produced by the National Film Board on the subject of poverty. As we all know, one person in five in this country lives in poverty. The reason I became a member of the Liberal Party is that I am convinced that in a technological age you cannot have true and small "c" conservatism because it is an anachronism that cannot work. In today's society you cannot adopt the philosophy of every man for himself and the devil take the hind-

I would suggest that the fact remains that our agricultural industry exists to sell these products, not to store them. If we have a critical problem of storage in this area, we have a serious problem that begs an answer. Some hon. members might feel that we have talked long enough about wheat and that we should get on with other things. I agree with that up to a point, but until we solve the problem and until we are able to get back our rightful share of world markets for agricultural products we have an obligation to keep talking, and we have an obligation to lay the governments consummate ineptitude out in the open and let the Canadian people pass judgment.
This budget appears to be designed to accomplish two objectives, both of which are suspect and both of which contain hidden and sinister portents of disaster. The first purpose was loudly proclaimed by the finance minister as a master-plan whereby the government and all other segments of the economy would cut back drastically on spending; that is, the government would cut back on expenditures and the private sector would cut back on buying. This, he admitted, would slow up the
DEBATES	5085
The Budget-Mr. Schumacher economic growth of the country and after a while, presto-no more inflation. Everyone would be suddenly healthier. The minister appeared to be surprised when he was told that the Canadian economy was already in a state of decline. After these last few years of Liberal rule, surely the last thing we should have to do now is artificially depress the Canadian economy.
There was no mention of housing in the budget, so presumably after a period of time there will suddenly be houses. There was no mention of poverty, so obviously everybody will be suddenly richer. There was no mention of wheat sales in this document, so we are left to conjure up visions of foreign buyers beating a path to our shores. These are beautiful visions, and I find it difficult to pull myself away from the intent of this document and back to the mundane world of reality. The realities, though, are quite different from this government's fantasies and pipe dreams. The reality of honest government is quite different from the tactic of bulldozing ill-conceived legislation through this House with completely misguided power.
The second hidden danger in the budget became immediately apparent when the finance minister proudly proclaimed that there were no new taxes or tariffs in this document. Even those guileless souls who dwell in the nether world of Liberal economic philosophy would not tumble to this little gambit. Why would those fearless plunderers on the other side of this House fail to take advantage of this golden opportunity to thrust their hands deeper into the pockets of the Canadian taxpayer, this flowing, bottomless well from whence all riches flow? Why should the Liberal tax grabbers spare the uncomplaining hordes of plundered and harried Canadian taxpayers? I suggest this is because there is a bigger haul in the offing; there is a bigger pot at the end of a brighter and gaudier rainbow. The lavish fiscal policies of this government should not be supported by a token gesture, by a mere several hundred million dollars. They are even now reeling under the public outcry over the scope of that iniquitous tax white paper, and this budget is calculated to smooth the ruffled feathers.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
It is calculated to deceive the unsuspecting victim into believing that he has been reprieved that that great federal tax axe is not going to fall. What a change of pace it would have been, what a refreshing breath of
March 16, 1970

The Budget-Mr. Schumacher sanity, if the government had announced that instead of the sham of offering "X" number of dollars to the farmers not to grow wheat it would use that money to subsidize the Canadian wheat market. What a stroke of genius it would have been had the government chosen to do the obvious.
Under the proposed system, called LIFT- which I believe translates into Lower Inventory for Tomorrow-we will end up with the same wheat we now have in abundance, plus the reduced new crop that will be harvested in the next season. Those acres not under cultivation will be in serious danger from the elements. I should not have to remind even the members of this House from eastern Canada of the effects of the last dust bowl tragedy that befell the Prairie provinces some years ago.
How much better it would have been had the government announced that it would overhaul the Canadian Wheat Board, revise its operating procedures, update its terms of reference and bring the grading system in line with other world wheat selling countries. Other wheat producing countries have changed their wheat marketing techniques and procedures to stay in the market. What good reason can the government give for failing to read the clear signs that other countries read and heed? If we are to be kept out of world markets because we will not change, what will it take to make us change? What will it take to make us wake up?
Some of the philosophical implications implicit in this budget, Mr. Speaker, are cause for alarm, and I suspect that they are indicative of panic. We are told that to solve the great economic problem of inflation it is necessary to add appreciably to the already serious problem of unemployment. Are we to extend this philosophy into other areas? If some sections of the country are depressed, should we depress the richer provinces until they are down to the level of the less fortunate? Should we cure ignorance by closing all schools in the country until all citizens are equally ignorant?
A close examination of any recent government legislation will prove that this is a dangerously valid analogy. It is beyond the grasp of a reasonable mind why the government, in the face of the critical, humanistic problems gripping our country today, should attempt to create stiU another federal agency and should provide still another drain on a strained economy, instead of facing up to its mandate.

We do not need a new agency to promote and foster the use of standards; we have a perfectly good standards agency already. Is this yet another smokescreen being thrown up by the government to take the public mind off the inanities in this budget, or to take some of the pressure off the campaign to ram the confiscatory tax reform legislation through this House? It seems strange to me, and I daresay to most members on both sides of this House, that one of the richest countries in the world cannot get along without repressive and suppressive economic policies.
It is a sad but true fact that this budget will be our economic guideline over the next few months. We wiU have to prop it up wherever possible and try to make it do. But I must go on record, Mr. Speaker, as being unalterably opposed to applying negative measures to solve positive problems. If the minister is expecting any bouquets for this latest budget, he can be assured that he will get them in abundance from this side of the House, but I must warn him that I sincerely hope he has a fondness for ragweed.

Mr. Speaker, I hope I will be able to complete my remarks in a very short time. I shall touch briefly on four aspects of policy; the budget as it has been presented to us, the associated austerity program, the white paper in so far as it relates to the matter before the House, and the present level of taxation in Canada.
Unfortunately, the minister is not here tonight. I believe he is in the counting house counting out his money. However, perhaps the most suitable thing I could do would be to quote for the minister the words of Franklin Pierce Adams who said, "Count that day when, turning on its axis, this earth imposes no additional taxes". At least this budget has the merit of being a considerable change from the pattern of Canadian governments from the days of the government of Louis St. Laurent. These previous governments consistently overspent. If there is one saying that could be applied to the many Liberal governments preceding this one, it would be one of Josh Billings whose advice was, "Live within your income even if you have to borrow money to do it".
Because the white paper is under discussion we realize that this budget is an interim measure. I do not think any of us were really surprised that it did not contain many changes. Speaking within that context, however, I congratulate this government without reservation for having the courage to impose
March 16, 1970	COMMONS
austerity on Canada and for having the courage to be unpopular, because we cannot amend the Canadian economy and we cannot curb inflation by following the policies of the past decade or 13 years of overspending.
Some government had to have the courage to tell the people that we can spend only what we take in and that preferably for some time we should spend less. I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) for reducing the public debt for the first time since 1957. I also congratulate him for bringing in a budget which contains no Ways and Means motion, the first of its kind in this nation since 1913.
I have spoken of what I consider to be the necessity in this country to curb spending and to curb taxes. I think it might be wise for hon. members of this House to consider who is curbing taxes and who is curbing spending, and what levels of government are not doing so. I have a few figures I should like to quote to the House from the report of the Tax Structure Committee of the Federal-Provincial Conference of Prime Ministers and Premiers on February 16 and 17, last month.
In 1952 the total tax take of Canada federally, provincially and municipally divided roughly into these percentages: 18 years ago in 1952 the federal revenue was 73 per cent, the provincial revenue was 15 per cent and the municipal revenue was 12 per cent. Then by 1956 there had been a considerable change; the federal share of the tax take was down to 69 per cent, the provincial revenue had increased to 18 per cent and the municipal revenue had increased by 1 per cent to 13 per cent. Then we come to the year 1960; the federal share was down to 62 per cent, the provincial share was up to 21 per cent and the municipal share was up to 16 per cent. For the year 1964 the relative figures are 57 per cent, 28 per cent and 15 per cent. In 1968 the federal share was 52 per cent, the provincial share was up to 33 per cent and the municipal share was 15 per cent.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
This paper, Mr. Speaker, was projected to 1971, and we find here again the federal government taking only 52 per cent of the tax revenue of Canada, the provinces continuing to increase their take to 35 per cent and the municipal groups, whom I think many members will agree are badly in need of more finances, down again to 13 per cent. Who is curbing spending in Canada and who is curbing taxation? Is it the federal government,

The Budget-Mr. St. Pierre whose share of the tax take has dropped from 73 per cent to 52 per cent, or the provincial governments whose share has risen from 15 per cent to 35 per cent?
These figures can be expressed in another way, as a percentage of the GNP in terms of taxation. These, of course, show the same thing in different figures-a steady decline in the federal government's rate of spending compared with the total national product. As to the total taxation load, this can be adjusted upward or downward even if the white paper is accepted in its entirety, which is highly unlikely, or whether the white paper is accepted in an amended form; or it can be done, as it is always done presently, under the taxation system as it exists now.
The level of taxation is not really a function of the white paper debate, but it is the general level of taxation on which I wish to speak for a few minutes. I think there is a real, legitimate concern, common to all members of the House as to what general level of taxation is supportable in this country before the initiative of individuals is stifled.
There are any number of people who are writing to hon. members telling them they know where it is, it is in the white paper, or else they claim it is not. Indeed, some of them who write leave me with the impression that the introduction of the graduated income tax in 1917 was the end of individual initiative in Canada. The facts do not appear to bear this out. But there is a point-I do not claim to know where it is; I do not know who the wise man could be who does know-beyond which taxation cannot rise.

Another hon. member says we have now reached that point-another wise man! I wish I had his omniscience. I am a simple man and I do not have answers to everything. I have the questions to which I seek answers.
The late Northcotte Parkinson claimed that the effective level of taxation was 10 per cent. He went further: it was his view that the ordinary citizen did not care if it was taken from him by the government he elected or by a bunch of bearded men who held the mountain pass. It was all the same to him; the 10 per cent was what he was willing to part with, whether to the robber for the government or to one of the freelance men of the woods.
We have long passed Mr. Parkinson's level. The taxation take of the three levels of government in Canada is now in the region of 35 or 36 per cent. We are told that in the United States it is far lower and that our young people will rush down to that happy land of health, wealth and high living as soon as any of the proposals of the white paper are introduced. However, the facts do not bear out that assertion. In 1969, 30 per cent of the American gross national product was going into the hands of various levels of government in taxes. In the last quarter of the last year the percentage of the American gross national product passing through the hands of the various levels of government reached, by odd coincidence, 35 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, can we indefinitely support taxation at 35, 36, 37 or up to 40 per cent? Where is the ceiling? We do not know, but I say we must always remain conscious of the fact that there is a ceiling. To me, every taxation can be likened to a cumulative poison-we are pretty sick before we find out we have had too much of it. We do not have the opportunity of rapidly comprehending the danger. It is not like stepping in front of a speeding truck where, if you make an error in judgment, the impact and punishment is immediate; it is more comparable to the ingestion of mercury poisoning in your food.
The taxpayer is not going to give the government clear notification of when he has had enough. He is not going to say, "Thirty-five per cent of my money you can take, but at 35.5 per cent I will stop paying." There will develop here a vague, persuasive discontent;
The Budget-Mr. Moore it will be a sickness. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this budget proposes to curb inflation. It may succeed in this to a degree, and it may not. What concerns me today is the tendency to disregard the problems of the non-urban sector of our economy which is in no way responsible for inflation. This area has, rather, been the victim of inflation. I do not want to leave the impression that I do not think urban areas have problems too, and very serious ones; I just want to deal with the area of the economy caught in the price squeeze.
One example of this unfairness, Mr. Speaker, is the closing of so many small post offices across the country. In many cases this may be justified. Many small offices close to a larger centre are no longer necessary. Their revenue has been dropping steadily and in some cases the villages surrounding them have all but disappeared. There are many cases, however, of rural post offices the revenue from which, though small, is increasing.
They serve not only as a post office but an important part of community life, possibly the only meeting place for neighbours. Most of these have been open for many years, and their removal has a serious effect, not only on the business with which they are usually associated but on their convenience to the patrons. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the saving of a few dollars in a department where money should not be the only criterion is not justified. The service to the community should have first consideration. To point out the chaos in that department I would refer to the headline in the Globe and Mail today stating "Postal Chaos in Montreal-Armed Guards to Move Mail if Necessary, Kierans Warns". This gives us a pretty fair idea of what is happening in the Post Office today.
Is it any wonder that there is concern and unrest in the rural areas of Canada? In the grain growing areas of the west, people are wondering what happened to the election promises of this government when the then agriculture minister promised to sell 4J million bushels of wheat annually for the next three years. That was in 1968. Now we

March 16, 1970
The Budget-Mr. Moore have a tremendous surplus of wheat and coarse grains built up in the Wheat Board designated area.
The recent announcement by the Minister without Portfolio in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) concerning the drastic reduction in wheat acreage is not well accepted by grain growers. They are aware, however, that at last the government has recognized their plight. For those who feel that this $100 million is a huge sum to pour into the western economy, it should be noted that it will have little effect on the many who practice mixed farming and are already diversified.
Other factors may determine its usefulness in the basically wheat growing areas. It may well be that only a small portion of the designated $100 million will be paid out. It is felt that under the so-called Lang-Olson formula, as little as $30 million or $40 million will go into the western economy. Grain farmers are worried about many aspects of this plan; for example, the land they have rented and agreed to farm in a good husbandlike order, also the problem of erosion involved in two or more years of consecutive summerfallowing.
Then we have the involved problems of the dairy industry, an industry affecting the local economy as well as the national economy of the country. It must be obvious by now to anyone concerned with the dairy industry that the government's recent dairy policies have failed to accomplish their intentions. It is all very well to say that the dairy industry should not be subsidized but should stand on its own feet. It would like to do that, Mr. Speaker. If dairymen were not producing a perishable product at a fixed price, often below the cost of production, they would not need a subsidy. They are operating in an economy wherein Canadian industry is subsidized by protective tariffs.
One fact of life that recent dairy policies have not taken into account is that in Canada we have large areas of deficit dairy production and other areas where production approximately equals demand. A dairy policy that does not take this into account fails to be realistic and discriminates against large areas of Canada. This was pointed out in submissions by a number of Canadian provinces, and cannot be ignored. The government would have us believe that the $10 million reduction in the allotment for dairy subsidy is part of the new austerity program. Rather, it is a continuation of a planned policy of

reducing the dairy subsidy, begun in 1967. It is my understanding that it is proposed to use the $10 million to finance the moving of the farmers off the farm.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
There is talk now of increasing the holdback on overquota milk, applying to both shippers of milk for manufacturing and fluid consumption. In the case of fluid producers there will be a straight decrease in price for that portion of a fluid shipper's milk that goes into the manufacturing market. This will be nothing less than a disaster for those whose fluid quota is a small percentage of their total production, and this applies to many top dairymen who ship to smaller points. They do not receive a subsidy in the first place, yet in the face of ever-increasing costs, they will be charged a holdback of 52 cents per 100 pounds of milk. Even more has been suggested, which will put these dairymen out of business.
Let us look for a moment at the advice the government gives to farmers. The advice is designed to solve their problems, and it is pretty ridiculous. To the dairymen the government says, "Expand your units, become more efficient, or in other words produce more." It also tells them, "Cut back on your production or we will make it so tough for you that you will be glad to get out of the business." How much sense does that make? To the farmers it says, "Expand your units; make them more viable. Grow more, but produce less. Diversify, but do not produce too much of anything because that product may become a drag on the market." What should the farmers grow? There is no answer. Perhaps they should grow flowers. This is the advice they are given in a world where many people are near starvation.
What are the government's plans for those who have already been forced off the land and the thousands more who will be? They are evidently to be moved from the land they love, out of the clean air and into the polluted air and congested environment of the cities. If history repeats itself, as it has a habit of doing, and we have another depression the government's advice will be, "Go back to the farm." It should not be surprised if the reply is, "What farm?" It is high time, Mr. Speaker, that we had some long-term planning in the whole field of agriculture. The productivity of our relatively small percentage of arable land in Canada should be considered a blessing, not a curse.

Mr. Speaker, the budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) last Thursday was an astounding document. Really, I have some difficulty understanding how the Minister of Finance could work up enough nerve to deliver such a budget speech. He made the point of suggesting that not since 1913 has there been a budget which has not been accompanied by any Ways and Means resolutions introducing tax or tariff changes. The fact is, of course, that the minister did not need to do this because he had already piloted through the House his tax and tariff increases for 1970.
But, more importantly, I suggest that not since 1913 have we had such a pitiful excuse for a budget. This budget reflects the fact that the Liberal government is paralyzed by its own contradictions and contradictory positions. The budget really is an amazing compilation of contradictions. The Minister of Finance as much as admitted that the government's anti-inflation policies have failed to work up to the present time. Just listen to this statement contained in the budget speech:
There are some recent glimmerings of evidence that the rate of Increase of prices is no longer rising.
What a statement that is, Mr. Speaker! It would seem that what the Minister of Finance is trying to say is that the rate of increase in the rate of price increases is no longer going up. Well, the glimmer promptly went out of the minister's financial vision. The Minister of Finance was not even left with a gleam or a flicker in his eye.

A colleague on my left has just said that there is no "love life" left. I do not think there will be much love for the Minister of Finance as a result of the word that went out last Friday that the consumer index had gone up by another half point and that it is now 5 per cent above the level of last year.
Hon. members will recall that in the budget address the Minister of Finance made a point of suggesting that on a national accounts basis the price increase factor for the past year was of the order of 4.2 per cent, and that the consumer price index had gone up by 4.6 per cent. The minister was saved by one day. If he had delivered his budget address just one day later, the word would have been out that the consumer price index had gone up to
The Budget-Mr. Burton 5 per cent over last year's level. The only thing the minister could offer was the pious hope that the policies that did not work in 1969 would work better in 1970. The minister blandly made this statement in his address:
-I anticipate some increase in unemployment.
That indicates that the minister decided to stand pat in terms of his economic policy, with the exception of the consumer credit controls which he introduced and which will have the effect of tightening the economic screws in Canada still further. This is the price Canadians will have to pay for a set of policies Which are not working, even if one were to accept them on a basis that a tradeoff between unemployment and deflation is acceptable. I do not accept that sort of proposition. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is morally wrong on the part of the government to tolerate and accept a higher level of unemployment as a price which Canadians have to pay for the government's so-called anti-inflation or deflationary policies.
Last fall the Minister of Finance appeared before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs and in answer to a question I posed said that he did not believe in the trade-off theory. The fact is that he has now put this trade-off theory into practice; he has put it into effect. He reminds me of an old-time buccaneer who simply said, "Damn the consequences; full sail ahead", or the captain of more recent years who said, "Damn the torpedos; full steam ahead." The Minister of Finance now says, "Damn the people; let them founder." It seems to me the Minister of Finance has lost all credibility. This loss in credibility cannot be summed up better than by the one sentence contained in his budget address of last Thursday, as follows:
We just cannot tell how soon or how far the slowing of growth in demand and in production will bring about a slowing down in price increases.
I do not understand how a Minister of Finance could have the nerve to make such a statement to the House of Commons, a statement which is a damning indictment of his economic policies, and not tender his resignation from his portfolio.

Another contradiction in the budget is the attitude of the Minister of Finance to business, and corporate business in particular, in contrast to his attitude toward consumers. The deferred capital allowances are continued, although no supporting information was offered or provided to show that they are working at the present time. Business has been left basically untouched by this budget. On the other hand, the government is nailing the consumer.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
I think one could question the effectiveness of the measures that were proposed, even on the basis that one accepted them. I think more fundamentally, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance and the government are tackling the wrong guy in the present situation. What they are trying to do is further restrict the people who are already feeling the pinch in our present economic situation. These new regulations will pose no problems for the people who have ample financial or economic resources, but to the extent these regulations and controls are effective they could slow down the economy even further than is now the case.
Why not control the financial institutions, their profits and interest rates? It seems that we are still following the bankrupt policies of the Prices and Incomes Commission instead of developing a comprehensive incomes policy. The minister should be aware that such a policy has the endorsement of this party. If he is not, I now draw his attention to it. This

was clearly set forth in a report which was submitted on behalf of the New Democratic Members of Parliament by the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. Saltsman) and myself as members of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. We called for the introduction of a comprehensive incomes policy as the only way out of the present situation. I wish to quote briefly from that report and the proposition that was put forward:
To achieve the objective of an equitable distribution of income and of an equitable distribution of the economic burden of rising prices, we propose a comprehensive incomes policy.
It is essential that what we mean by an incomes policy be well understood. To be meaningful, it must be comprehensive, it must include all forms of income. In addition to wages and salaries (the salaries of Members of Parliament included) all forms of non-wage and non-salary income-including profits, rents, interest, professional fees and unincorporated business income must be subject to the policy.
The comprehensive incomes policy must include the provision of a guaranteed annual income, to avoid injustice and hardship. It must be flexible enough to take account of: (1) the plight of low-paid workers (2) disparities within industries and classes of employees (3) increases in the cost of living and (4) other factors causing disadvantage to groups or regions.
It will take time to develop a comprehensive incomes policy fully. Constitutional, economic and geographic factors make it more difficult to apply such a policy in Canada than in some countries. We will have to learn lessons through experience. But the objective and the need are clear. The best way to get there is to start now.
That is the end of the quotation which I submit for the consideration of all members of this House. A further failing of this budget which poses another contradiction is that nothing is being done, and nothing is proposed, to slow down the rate of take-over of the Canadian economy by foreign interests or the dependence of the economy on foreign developments and events. I will deal with this point further on another occasion. It is generally agreed, and it is quite clear, that some of the events to which Canada is subject take place in foreign countries and are in fact beyond our effective control.
In summary, I suggest that the government has demonstrated its incapacity to manage the economy in the interest of Canadians. I wish to give a short and brief analysis of some of my reasons for coming to this conclusion. The first point is that the government does not recognize changes that have taken place in the Canadian economy. The fact is that our economy is no longer governed by market forces, the laws of supply and demand

as we have known them. They cannot do the job now or in the future.
We are living in an economy which is featured by administered prices for the most part. Corporate power, including international and multinational corporate power, controls much of our economy and in fact will be an important influence in the future. One example of the fact that we must realize Canada is living in a new economic situation is exemplified by current developments. At the present time we have a rate of unemployment that based on actual figures is over 6 per cent. We have a rate of price increase in the area of 5 per cent.

The government is willing to risk a recession for the sake of carrying on its present policies which are not working. I plead with the government to take another look at its policies. For this reason I welcomed the announcement last week that several areas in Saskatchewan are to be included among the special areas established by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. This will certainly give a psychological boost to the province. Regina and Saskatoon have been included in addition to an area in the Meadow Lake district. It remains to be seen to what extent this new program will be used. Until last week nothing had been done in those areas of Saskatchewan which had been declared eligible under the regional incentives legislation. There are many parts of Saskatchewan which are deserving of further assistance. I stand by my original contention that the entire province should be declared a designated area under the Regional Development Incentives Act. It seems to me that in Saskatchewan at the present time we are handicapped by the worst combination which could be encountered, that is, a Liberal government in Ottawa and a Liberal government in Regina.
In Ottawa we have a Liberal government which has demonstrated, for the most part, little concern for the province. In Regina we have a Liberal government which is desperately trying to pick a fight with Ottawa as its only means of survival in the next election: they know they cannot survive on the basis of their record. This is illustrated by a little

squabble which took place last week. It seems there is to be a new distillery built in Wey-burn. We are very happy about this. But the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) from Saskatchewan and the Premier of the province could not help getting into a squable about who should make the announcement. The Premier was to make the announcement on Friday morning, but I gather the Minister without Portfolio felt he should get there first so he made the announcement on Thursday evening, beating the Premier to the post. This is an indication of the petty squabbling which is going on between the Liberals in Regina and those in Ottawa. The people of Saskatchewan are suffering as a consequence.
Further programs are needed to improve farm income, in addition to a generous public works program in the province and an energetic continuation of regional development plans. The people of Saskatchewan are greatly concerned about what is happening in agriculture at the present time. Agriculture is one of the worst of the trouble spots in the economy and the attitude of the government has been one of reacting to a crisis. There have been many examples of this over the past year and a half. The most recent was the announcement of the wheat acreage reduction program called LIFT-Lower Inventory For Tomorrow. Many farmers in western Canada would like to give it a different sort of lift. This is not an income plan, Mr. Speaker. It is an incentive plan to persuade farmers not to produce in 1970. It represents a complete turnabout as compared with the policy put forward a few years ago when farmers were urged to grow all they could. Now the farmers have to pay the shot for following the government's policy.
This program has certain basic shortcomings. First, it is poor psychology. It does not wear well with farmers to ask them not to produce. For this reason the policy will be ignored by many farmers in western Canada simply because it is not realistically related to their situation. Second, there are basic inequities in the program, the most obvious of which relate to the situation of farmers who made a considerable adjustment last year and who are now penalized as a consequence. Third, the plan fails to take into account the social and economic consequences.
I don't believe this program was subjected to a cost-benefit analysis before it was announced. If any minister disagrees with this statement, I challenge him to table whatever studies were prepared in the development of

this program. I contend there are serious potential environmental problems associated with the program. Suppose we encounter a dry year with low rainfall; we could find ourselves in a serious situation. Crop scientists have already warned farmers about this possibility and have expressed concern. Fifth, there are no income alternatives presented to farmers and, sixth, the plan does not take into account the situation of small farmers and mixed farmers.
The program is an example of the trouble we get into when policies are made by a minister or ministers who may be intelligent or capable but who lack an understanding of, or a feeling for the agricultural industry and rural people. I am only telling the House what was told me by good Conservative constituents, friends of hon. gentlemen to my left.
I want to devote a few minutes to what has been said by others who have preceded me. First of all, I go back to what the financial critic for the New Democratic Party said. In my opinion, he was most unfair in his criticism this afternoon of the Liberal government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson). I do not contend that there is some reason why a member of the New Democratic Party should not be unfair, but I do say that the hon. member was not realistic in his approach to a subject that is of most importance to the people of Canada.
For example, the hon. member spoke of regional development and said this was good, that the government to the right of Mr. Speaker was doing an excellent job. Then he said that it was not good so long as we did not have full employment. I am sure there is no one in the government or on the Liberal benches who does not wish there were full employment in Canada today. Everybody wants full employment. But what happens if we price ourselves completely out of world markets? I realize that our friends in the New Democratic Party do not agree that we might in the future price ourselves out of world markets, but what would happen if we did? Then we would really have unemployment. The choice is not between inflation and unemployment. The government by its actions is showing it is against inflation and that it hopes to be able to do something about the problem.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
The government is also against unemployment, but the brutal fact is that it must make a choice, not about unemployment today but unemployment five years from now. What about unemployment two years from now? Is it not better to have 5 per cent of the people unemployed today, cruel though it may be, than to have 10 per cent of our people unemployed two or three years from now? This is the struggle and these are the questions that are going through the mind of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) as he works on this problem which is very serious to him and indeed to all the people of Canada. It is all very easy to be on the left of Mr. Speaker, as indeed I am, and to be somewhat critical of the government. But when you sit in high
March 16, 1970

places and you are the Minister of Finance responsible for raising $12 billion or $13 billion, and at the same time you must look after the spending of $12 billion or $13 billion, it is a more difficult job than criticizing all the time.
My friend the hon. member for Waterloo asks what is the cost of unemployment in Canada. May I be the first to tell him that it costs a great deal of money. I agree with my friend when he suggested that perhaps it costs in the neighbourhood of $4 billion per year. This is a situation we should all strive to rectify. No one wants unemployment and no one wants inflation. But inflation is not just a problem in Canada: it is not just a problem facing the government which sits opposite; it is a problem of all Canadians and, indeed, all the world. There is as much inflation in the United States as there is here. We are bound to have more inflation in a country that is going ahead faster than any other, for example Japan. There is now inflation in Germany, the other country that lost the war.
We are a small country in population, with approximately 21 million people. The Minister of Finance is the man who has to come up with the answers and I appreciate the difficulty he faces. He is faced with unemployment which costs a great deal, and it will cost a great deal more if we do not attack the inflationary situation which exists not only in this country but indeed in the whole world.
The hon. member for Waterloo suggested that the government has caused unemployment. I deny that completely. The government has not caused unemployment. What the government is attempting to do is solve the inflationary situation. In my opinion it is one of the greatest forms of robbery we could have in this country. Some time ago I referred to the devaluation situation. Supposing a fellow retired ten years ago with $50,000 in bonds, perhaps a farmer from Quebec or Ontario, or with $100,000 if he happened to own a profitable wheat farm in Saskatchewan, and supposing he put his money on deposit with the Royal Bank of Canada or in Canadian government bonds: today that money would be worth only about half what is was worth ten years ago. Inflation is a tremendous robber. This is a problem not only in Canada but throughout the world, and it must be beaten because neither Canada nor the world can afford it. While we are interested in the world situation, we are primarily interested in this Canada of ours.
