speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 2 I posed the following question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp):
In view of the fact that Canada sold approximately $300 million worth of weapons and defence materials to the United States in 1969, is the Canadian government now considering putting an end to this complicity in the Viet Nam war by stopping these sales?
I asked this question for a number of reasons. I would preface my remarks by saying that Canada is by far the largest foreign supplier of military equipment to the United States. Let me use a couple of very simjple statistics to show what I mean. In 1964 we sold about $161 million worth of war and military equipment to the United States; in 1969 we sold them approximately $300 million worth of defence and military equipment. In 1964, six years ago, there were approximately 23,000 United States troops in Viet Nam; in 1969 there were over 500,000 United States troops in Viet Nam, and over half a million United States troops are fighting in Viet Nam today.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
As we know, the defence-sharing agreement is one whereby specific military equipment is contracted for by the Pentagon. We know that much of this equipment which goes to the United States is used directly in the war in Viet Nam: this has been stated by people in the Pentagon. Any of this equipment which does not go directly to Viet Nam finds its way into the United States military pot. This means that indirectly that we have equipment there, because the United States can use more of its equipment in Viet Nam, so it really does not make much difference.
[Mr. Whicher.)

I should like to see Canada out of this type of involvement. Whether or not we are in favour of the war in Viet Nam, we are involved whether we like it or not because we are supplying military equipment and military goods to the United States. Viet Nam has perhaps done more than anything else to divide the generations in America. If we look around in the United States, and even in Canada today, we can see that it has divided societies, communities and families.
I maintain that the United States presence in Viet Nam is politically and morally wrong. In being involved in a war in Viet Nam the United States is leaving one of the deepest scars on the conscience of humanity. It is an aggressive war. It is being fought by a foreign power against a people who for decades have been fighting powers such as China, France and now the United States.
Let us for a moment look at Canada's role in the Viet Nam war. I think it is very inconsistent in respect of our stand in other wars which are going on now or which have gone on in the last few years. We did not supply arms to either side in India or Pakistan. We are not supplying arms to either Israel or the Arab states. We did not supply arms to either Nigeria or Biafra regardless of our activity or inactivity in that situation. In all these situations we maintained a degree of military neutrality. We are not doing that in the case of Viet Nam because we are supplying approximately $300 million worth of arms to the United States this year and supplied more, as a matter of fact, during the last two years.
Ending the war in Viet Nam is something we alone cannot do-we all realize that-but we can make a contribution to that end. One way to do it is by cutting off our supply of arms to the United States. This would contribute to ending the killing and misery which is going on in Viet Nam today. It would also help the United States get out of this war in Asia because, as I have said, it not only is dividing the people but is placing the United States in the position of being a giant powder keg which is ready to explode at any time.
The United States involvement in Viet Nam has many other detrimental effects. It is draining the United States economy of money which could be spent on housing, on combating poverty and in cleaning up the cities of that country. These things, too, contribute to the very explosive situation in the United States. It is also in the interest of Canada that the war end as soon as possible, because whether we like it or not the Viet Nam war is
March 16, 1970	COMMONS
contributing to everything from inflation to social unrest in this country. No matter what we think of it or how we like it, this is the way it is. We must try to stop that war as soon as possible.
I do not think any Canadians like to think they are a part of the killing and misery which is going on in a far away rice paddy at this very moment. Finally, if we do stop the sale of armaments to the United States, or through the United Nations put pressure on all sides to stop the fighting, we will indeed strengthen the international community. How many more Yiet Nams or Nigeria-Biafras will it take before the world will suddenly blow up? How many more situations like this can we tolerate before that final spark, and before there is a major nuclear confrontation with which we would have to contend? For these reasons, in brief, I was asking and am asking the government to stop our sale of arms to the United States.

There are others who disapprove, too. But what he is suggesting is that because he and many Canadians disagree with the war in Viet Nam, this country should end its long-standing defence arrangements with the United States. In the first place, the great bulk of United States procurement in Canada under these arrangements does not consist of weapons but electronic equipment, transport aircraft and various components and materials.
In the second place, Canadian-made equipment goes into the general inventory of the United States armed forces and may be used by those forces anywhere in that country or overseas. As an ally of the United States in North America and in NATO, I think it is entirely appropriate that we should have such defence production-sharing arrangements. It is therefore quite misleading on the part of the hon. member to suggest that Canadian weapons are being supplied to the United States for use in Viet Nam. Some of them may be used there but the defence production arrangement, as he himself has mentioned in his remarks, predates any involvement by the

We have a two-way arrangement with the United States under which we purchase considerable quantities of modem defence equipment for the Canadian armed forces, and we seek to balance this by sales to U.S. agencies. There have been times when the balance has been more in favour of Canada and other times when it has been more in favour of the United States. It has varied from time to time. At the moment I guess it is more favourable to us.
The government is not contemplating the ending of this defence production-sharing agreement with the United States. To do so would be a reversal of the whole co-operative defence relationship and would be costly as well to Canadian industry and to Canadian workers, to no good purpose.

Did the provincial governments submit briefs on the subject of pollution control to the federal government during the federal-provincial conference held in Ottawa on February 16 and 17? If so, why has the minister not made these briefs available to the national resources committee which is currently dealing with the Canada Water Act?
The minister gave no reply to the question, and because it is of vital importance to the national resources committee, which is now studying the new legislation, I asked that it be raised at this time. During our committee meeting on February 3, the minister indicated that points of discussions between the federal government and the provinces would not be passed on to the committee. Two weeks later the Federal-Provincial Conference took place in Ottawa.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
The provinces submitted briefs to the federal government on their views and approach to the pollution problems facing Canada. I feel these briefs should be passed on to the National Resources Committee for study and action. It is the only sensible way of acquainting the committee members with the problems facing us under the new Canada Water Act. To date, this information has not been given to the committee despite the assurance of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on February 18 that the provincial briefs had been made public.
How can the Standing Committee of the House of Commons on National Resources do an adequate job of amending legislation which is currently before it, when the information on problems which we are facing provincially is not made available to the members for study? This is an odd way of making sensible legislation. I trust this attitude on the part of the minister will not continue and that all the material available will be released to the committee. We all want to make the new act workable and we must have the necessary background material to do this.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to pose two questions to the minister: Will copies of the briefs be made available to all members of the committee and, if so, when?
